questions.q: According to this lesson, what four questions should a good data quality scorecard answer for each metric?
options: Current value, good or bad against a threshold, trend over time, and who owns it
Table name, column name, data type, and row count
Who wrote the rule, when it was written, how long it took, and its SQL text
Server name, database name, schema name, and table size
questions.explain: Those four questions turn a raw number into something a non-technical stakeholder can act on.

questions.q: In the Power BI Scorecards hub screenshot shown in this lesson, what does each scorecard tile display?
options: A current value, a target, a trend line, and a status pill (such as On track or At risk)
Only a single red or green dot with no other detail
The raw SQL query behind the metric
A list of every individual row that failed a check
questions.explain: The tiles shown combine current value/target, a trend sparkline, and a colored status pill — the core scorecard pattern.

questions.q: Is Power BI's Goals feature, shown in this lesson's screenshots, a data-quality-specific product?
options: No — it's a general-purpose business goal-tracking feature used here as an example of the scorecard pattern
Yes — it was built exclusively for tracking data quality metrics
Yes — it can only connect to data quality rule results
No — it has no concept of a target or status at all
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that Goals is a general business-tracking tool whose current-value/target/status/trend structure applies well to data quality metrics, not a dedicated data quality product.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a scorecard and a dashboard, as described in this lesson?
options: A scorecard answers 'are we on track' at a glance for executives; a dashboard provides the detailed breakdowns and drill-through an analyst needs to investigate
A dashboard only works with manual data; a scorecard only works with automated data
They are identical, just different names for the same thing
A scorecard always shows more detail than a dashboard
questions.explain: A healthy program typically needs both: a scorecard for quick status and a dashboard underneath it for investigation.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend that scorecard status thresholds match the tolerances from Lesson 21?
options: A scorecard that disagrees with the thresholds people use to triage issues erodes trust in the scorecard fast
It's a technical requirement of Power BI's Goals feature
Thresholds from Lesson 21 are hard-coded into every BI tool automatically
There is no real connection between thresholds and scorecard design
questions.explain: Consistency between what the scorecard shows as 'at risk' and what actually triggers an issue keeps the scorecard credible.
